title: Injecting Services into Components 💉
description: Use constructor injection to bring a service to life and share data between components.

slides.title: Dependency Injection (DI) – The Magic 🪄
slides.content:
# How Angular Gives Your Component What It Needs

Angular’s DI system automatically creates and delivers service instances to components that ask for them.

1. You declare a dependency in the component’s constructor.
2. Angular looks at the parameter type, finds the matching provider, creates the service (if not already created), and passes it in.
3. You don’t need to `new` anything – Angular handles the entire lifecycle.

This decouples your component from the service implementation.

slides.title: The Constructor Parameter Shorthand 🧼

quizData.question: How do you tell Angular that a component needs a service?

options.text: List it in the component's `providers` array.
Declare it as a property with `@Service`.
Add it as a constructor parameter with a type.

quizData.explanation: Angular uses the constructor parameter type to know what to inject.

slides.title: Sharing Data Between Components via a Service
slides.content:
Since a service is a singleton, two components can use it to share state.

Step 1: Create a service with a shared property.

slides.content: Component A sets the message, Component B reads it.

slides.title: The Service Is the Same Instance 🔄
slides.content:
When ComponentA calls `setMessage`, ComponentB will see the change because they share the exact same instance of `DataService`.

This is a simple yet powerful pattern for cross‑component communication – no need for `@Input`/`@Output` chains when the components are not directly parent‑child.

quizData.question: Two components that inject the same service (providedIn: 'root') get different instances of that service.
quizData.explanation: With `providedIn: 'root'`, the service is a singleton – one instance shared across the app.

slides.title: Avoid Overusing Services for All State ⚠️
slides.content: While services are great for shared state, don’t turn them into a giant global variable bag. For complex state, consider state management libraries (NgRx, Akita) or simple RxJS stores (Chapter 10).
